title: Sting-Narrated Documentary About ‘The Godfather,’ ‘La Dolce Vita’ Composer Nino Rota Boarded by Global Constellation (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Vuelta’s sales and finance outfit Global Constellation has boarded international sales on “Nino: A Film About Nino Rota,” a documentary exploring th
body:
Vuelta’s sales and finance outfit Global Constellation has boarded international sales on “Nino: A Film About Nino Rota,” a documentary exploring the life and legacy of the Oscar-winning Italian composer, ahead of its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, where it will screen in the Official Selection Out of Competition.

	Directed by Walter Fasano, the longtime editor of Luca Guadagnino’s films (“Call Me by Your Name,” “Suspiria”), “Nino: A Film About Nino Rota” adopts a “free and associative narrative form to explore the personal, artistic and spiritual ties that shaped his life, revealing an artist who dedicated himself entirely to music and the ideals it embodies,” according to a statement.
	

	Narrated by 17-time Grammy Award winner Sting, the documentary brings together interviews with leading figures from the worlds of cinema and music, including Oscar-winning composer Alexandre Desplat, filmmaker Park Chan-wook, Grammy-winning composer and arranger Vince Mendoza, and many others, offering a “vivid portrait of Rota’s creative universe and the profound influence he continues to exert on filmmakers and composers today.”


	Rota composed the music for Francis Ford Coppola’s “The Godfather” and “The Godfather Part II,” for which he won an Academy Award. He is also known for his collaboration with Federico Fellini across much of the filmmaker’s career, including such masterpieces as “La Dolce Vita,” “8½” and “Amarcord,” and he composed the music for Luchino Visconti’s “The Leopard.”

	“Nino: A Film About Nino Rota” is produced by Be Water Film (Mattia Guerra), Sugar Play (Filippo Sugar, Elisabetta Biganzoli), Adler Entertainment (Marco Colombo), I Diavoli, Marco Morabito and Fasano in collaboration with Rai Documentari, and with the support of MIC-DGCA Fondo per lo sviluppo degli investimenti nel cinema e nell’audiovisivo, Apulia Film Fund, Apulia Film Commission and Regione Puglia.
	

	Be Water Film and Adler Entertainment will co-release the film in Italy.

	Fasano has edited more than 70 films, collaborating with directors such as Park Chan-wook, Dario Argento, the D’Innocenzo brothers and Trudie Styler. His collaborations with Guadagnino include “The Protagonists,” “I Am Love” (which Fasano also co-wrote), “A Bigger Splash,” “Suspiria” and “Bertolucci on Bertolucci,” which they co-directed. He shared the David di Donatello for best adapted screenplay for “Call Me by Your Name,” written with Guadagnino and James Ivory. The film went on to receive four Academy Award nominations and won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay.

	In 2021, Fasano wrote and directed “Pino,” a documentary on the artist Pino Pascali, which won best documentary at the Turin Film Festival.

title: Online Sleuthing Is Out of Control, and the Vitriol Against Patrick Clancy Proves It
description: The trial of Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse who admitted to strangling her three young children before attempting suicide in Janu
body:
The trial of Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse who admitted to strangling her three young children before attempting suicide in January 2023, has become the latest true crime sensation largely due to social media. Amateur sleuths, armchair lawyers and influencers have turned the soon-to-conclude trial into snackable, whodunit content, dissecting every detail and advancing their own theories across TikTok and other social platforms.
	

	Rather than focusing on the established facts — particularly Lindsay Clancy’s own admission that she killed her children — a growing number of internet investigators have cast her ex-husband and the children’s father, Patrick Clancy, as the villain. The murderer.



	“He was having an affair, he plotted, drugged her, made her crazy, killed their kids. Tried to kill her. When she didn’t die, he convinced her he killed them. Framed her. Sent her to prison,” one Instagram user wrote in a widely shared post.

	In a TikTok video posted on Aug. 17, Lisa Rinna, the former star of “The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills,” said, “All right, he did it. Patrick did it. Patrick’s the one who did it. Not Lindsay. Patrick did it. Because, you know, I also heard that women typically don’t strangle.”

	But the Lindsay Clancy case is not a cold case. There is no mystery to be solved. Lindsay did it.


	She’s on trial because prosecutors argue that Clancy, 36, was clear-minded when she planned and carried out the killings. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argues that she was overprescribed psychiatric medications and was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Jurors are currently deliberating on whether Clancy spends the rest of her life in prison or in a locked, state-run psychiatric facility.


	Whatever the verdict, the Massachusetts mother’s story will almost certainly become entertainment fodder soon enough. As Page Six Hollywood reported today, “numerous studios and streamers are interested in bringing Clancy’s story and trial to the screen.” And rumors are circulating that a well-known documentarian is currently making a documentary about the case. Others are likely to follow in his footsteps, because docs about the worst day of someone’s life and the terrible things people do to one another is a genre of entertainment that audiences can’t get enough of. Netflix docs “Crash,” “Maternal Instinct” and “Unknown Number: The High School Catfish” each spent time on the platform’s Top 10 chart this year. Earlier this month, “The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare” garnered 18.2 million views in its first week on Netflix.No one in the courtroom is debating Patrick Clancy’s guilt or innocence. But that still hasn’t stopped online communities from perpetuating harmful theories about him.

	Included among those theories: Lindsay was “shaking” when she saw Patrick walk into the courtroom to testify, and therefore, she was scared of him during their marriage. Patrick took his eldest child skiing after dropping Lindsay off at a mental institution, which means he didn’t care about his wife’s mental state. Patrick was an absentee father because he worked so much. (He was the only source of income for the family of five at the time of his children’s murders.) Patrick was a narcissist, because after Lindsay told him, and notably her mother, that she was suffering from postpartum depression and feared harming her children, he brunched with friends and took a two-day trip to New York (it’s unclear whether that was for work or not). But what citizen detectives hate the most is that Patrick moved on too quickly: He remarried earlier this year.

	“The ONLY way I would consider marrying a man whose ex-wife supposedly murdered their 3 children and is now on trial for it….. is if I was already with him before it happened,” reads one Facebook comment.

	Here’s another: “Dude, just hear me out. Patrick Clancy was cheating on Lindsay for at least 3 known years before the murders took place.Kathryn Coduto, a professor of media science at Boston University who studies social media and true crime, said the online effort to put Patrick Clancy on trial in the court of public opinion reflects a desire for a more familiar, coherent narrative.
	

	“Some people want this case to fit in really neatly with others and part of what that entails is an expectation that men are more likely to be perpetrators,” said Coduto. True crime, she noted, has a particularly large audience among women, many of whom consume it to understand “how to not be a victim.”

	“So, when you look at this case, to have a woman, and not just a woman, but a mother, saying, ‘Yes, I murdered my three kids,’ that’s really hard for people to accept. It doesn’t fit into the neat worldview that they have created around true crime.”

	Crime is hardly a new obsession, of course. In 1892, the trial of Lizzie Borden, who was accused of murdering her father and stepmother with an ax, became a national sensation. Her notoriety and the public’s fascination with the case, some historians have argued, led to Borden’s acquittal. Decades later, Truman Capote’s 1966 book, “In Cold Blood,” which chronicled the brutal and seemingly inexplicable murders of a Kansas family of four, became a bestseller, and is considered to have started the true crime genre. And on Oct. 3, 1995, an estimated 150 million Americans — roughly 57% of the country — tuned in to watch the verdict in the O.J. Simpson murder trial.

	One argument for televising the Simpson trial was that cameras would give the public an unfiltered view of the proceedings, without relying on third-party accounts. But even that case was riddled with conspiracy theories, including one that accused Simpson’s son Jason of killing his stepmom and her friend. But social media has dramatically changed the way people consume true crime over the past three decades, replacing a passive viewing with a constant stream of commentary, speculation and reactions unfolding in real time.

	“It’s really easy to watch something from the third person and feel like you would know better, or you would have done something differently,” said Coduto. “If you come up with a theory, a conspiracy, or if you have an idea of what might have happened, you can log on anytime, and you can see what other clues people have found. You can throw your own ideas in there.”

	For some, she said, there is an added incentive, she added: “There are a lot of people on social media hoping that their one video will take off and go viral.”
	

	Documentaries like Netflix’s “Don’t F**k With Cats” and “Crime Scene: The Vanishing at the Cecil Hotel,” and HBO Max’s “They Called Him Mostly Harmless” highlight online communities that have played a role by identifying clues, tracing identities or helping piece together what happened.

	But the Lindsay Clancy case is not a cold case. There is no mystery to be solved. 

	“For every case, there’s the real trial, and there’s the social media trial,” said criminal defense attorney Peter Elikann. “It has become almost a staple. But as far as the rumors of Patrick Clancy, it just seems like there isn’t one iota of evidence whatsoever at all to back this up. Lindsay’s attorney, an extraordinarily talented counsel, has said that she [Lindsay] was the one who did it.”

	To repeat: Lindsay Clancy’s own lawyer has said she killed her children.

	In a GoFundMe started in 2023 to raise money for his murdered children’s funerals, Patrick Clancy wrote: “I want to share some thoughts about Lindsay. She’s recently been portrayed largely by people who have never met her and never knew who the real Lindsay was. Our marriage was wonderful and diametrically grew stronger as her condition rapidly worsened. I took as much pride in being her husband as I did in being a father and felt persistently lucky to have her in my life. I to forgive Lindsay.” In a New Yorker article published in October 2024, Patrick told a reporter that he “wasn’t married to a monster – I was married to someone who got sick.”

	His support of his ex-wife has been twisted around by citizen detectives who have accused Patrick of money-grabbing.
	


	“Patrick Clancy walked out of this as a millionaire,” reads yet another Facebook comment. “He got $1.7 million in GoFundMe, sold the house and kept all the sale proceeds and has an active civil lawsuit against hospitals and docs who treated her which I’m sure will settle for millions considering the publicity around the case. So he got his new wife, new baby and became a multimillionaire for being an absentee father and husband. He failed his wife and his children.”Amateur sleuths’ attempt to destroy an innocent person’s life is also nothing new.

	During the Idaho college murders investigation in 2022, strangers online sleuths raced to identify a suspect long before Bryan Kohberger was caught (and pleaded guilty) for fatally stabbing Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle. Speculation about how the killings unfolded, why it happened and who was responsible spread rapidly across social media, fueling conspiracy theories that resulted in several innocent people being harassed and, in some cases, falsely accused.


	Bethany Funke and Dylan Mortensen, the surviving roommates of the four slain victims, faced severe online harassment and death threats from trolls following the murders. These unfounded leaps of logic can have real-world repercussions: In February 2026, a federal jury ordered influencer Ashley Guillard to pay University of Idaho professor Rebecca Scofield $10 million in damages for falsely claiming on TikTok that Scofield was responsible for the murders.

	There’s also the example of the murder trial of Karen Read, which became a media sensation, after she was charged with the 2022 death of her Boston police officer boyfriend John O’Keefe. O’Keefe’s family and friends Jennifer McCabe, Brian Albert, Colin Albert and Brian Higgins allege that Read worked with Aidan Kearney, the blogger known as “Turtleboy,” to falsely implicate them in the death of John O’Keefe. That lawsuit is still playing out in the courts.

	When the Lindsay Clancy trial concludes soon, Patrick Clancy will remain a free man, regardless of online speculation about his guilt. Whether or not the man who lost his three children will continue to be abused online is anyone’s guess.

title: Netflix Orders ‘Manifest’ Spinoff ‘Arrivals,’ With a New Mystery and Cast — Announced on 8/28, Of Course
description: “Manifest,” the drama series about a plane that mysteriously disappeared and then returned five and a half years later — with none of its passengers
body:
“Manifest,” the drama series about a plane that mysteriously disappeared and then returned five and a half years later — with none of its passengers aging — is about to get a sequel. Netflix announced Friday that it has given a greenlight to “Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery,” a new sci-fi spinoff that comes from the team behind the original series.

	Helming “Arrivals” will be original “Manifest” creator and showrunner Jeff Rake, who will be joined by original series co-executive producers Margaret Easley and Laura Putney, who will serve now as co-creators and co-showrunners as well. Warner Bros. TV is the studio.
	

	Here’s the new logline: “When a mysterious plane crash-lands in Denver, the passengers emerge with no memory of who they are, where they came from, or why they’re here. A young social worker and a novice Homeland Security agent team up with the new arrivals in an attempt to stop a humanity-ending catastrophe, discovering along the way that they are all part of the very puzzle they’re trying to solve.”


	Netflix, of course, chose Aug. 28 at 8:28 a.m. to announce the show for a very specific reason: “Manifest” was all about Flight 828 (8/28, get it?), and those numbers took on significant meaning during the series run. 

	“We are thrilled to expand the ‘Manifest’ universe with ‘Arrivals,’ led by the original creative team of Jeff Rake, Margaret Easley and Laura Putney,” Jinny Howe, Netflix head of scripted series, US & Canada, said in a statement. Their return ensures the creative continuity essential to this franchise, allowing us to honor what made the original a phenomenon while introducing a fresh perspective for fans worldwide.”
	

	“Manifest” originally launched on NBC in September 2018, starred Melissa Roxburgh, Josh Dallas, Athena Karkanis, J.R. Ramirez, Luna Blaise, Jack Messina, Parveen Kaur, Matt Long and Holly Taylor. NBC canceled the show after three seasons in 2021, but then Netflix picked it up for a fourth and final season. 

	On Netflix, Season 4 was released in two drops: 10 episodes on Nov. 4, 2022, followed by the final 10 on June 2, 2023. According to Netflix, all four seasons of “Manifest” have garnered more than 130 million views since the first half of 2023. It noted that Season 4 “spent 9 weeks in the Global Top 10 English TV list and hit #1 in over 90 countries tracked.”



	

					Jeff Rake, Margaret Easley, Laura Putney
	



	“When the idea for ‘Manifest’ first crash-landed in my head, I never imagined where it would lead,” Rake said in a statement. “What started as a wild concept became something much bigger — a story that connected with millions of people around the globe. And thanks to Netflix, we were able to finish the journey and give those fans the ending they deserved.

	“But the world of ‘Manifest’ has more stories to tell,” he added. “To now bring fans a brand-new mystery from that world is quite simply beyond my wildest dreams. ‘Arrivals’ co-creators and co-showrunners Laura Putney and Margaret Easley have been my trusted colleagues for over a decade. Their contribution to the ‘Manifest’ mothership cannot be overstated. It was a no-brainer to make them my partners on this spinoff. Together we’ve set out to create something bold, surprising, deeply human, and full of the kind of big ideas that spark conversations long after the credits roll. We can’t wait for a whole new audience — and longtime ‘Manifest’ fans — to discover ‘Arrivals.’”

	Besides Rake, Easley and Putney, other executive producers include Robert Zemeckis (“Forrest Gump,” “Back to the Future”) and Jack Rapke (“Cast Away,” “Flight”) of Compari Entertainment; Len Goldstein (“Hart of Dixie”) of Tall Baby Productions (which has an overall deal with Warner Bros. TV) and Jacqueline Levine (“Project Blue Book”).

title: Not Your Daddy’s Films Expands With Film Independent as Fiscal Sponsor (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Not Your Daddy’s Films, a social impact organization focused on educating and elevating women and nonbinary filmmakers, is now fiscally sponsored by
body:
Not Your Daddy’s Films, a social impact organization focused on educating and elevating women and nonbinary filmmakers, is now fiscally sponsored by Film Independent, the non-profit independent media arts organization.

	News of the partnership comes as Not Your Daddy’s Films celebrates its fourth anniversary. The Los Angeles-based organization was founded in 2022 by Kourtney Bell, Katherine Hughes, Nicole Lipp, Vika Stubblebine and Carlye Tamaren — five multi-hyphenates who were “frustrated by the persistent lack of gender equity and diversity behind the camera.”
	

	“We started NYDF because we wanted the kind of community we weren’t finding anywhere else… ambitious, accessible and actually fun to be part of,” the founders said in a joint statement. “Becoming a fiscally sponsored project of Film Independent means we can take the momentum we’ve built over the last four years and continue to uplift and empower filmmakers, without losing the energy that made people want to show up in the first place.”




	

									Annie Noelker
	



	NYDF began as a bimonthly screening for 25 people, and has since grown into a thriving “Daddy community” with events drawing more than 300 attendees. Over the last four years, the organization has hosted screenings, workshops, panels and parties spotlighting women and nonbinary filmmakers, and partnered with industry institutions including the American Cinematheque, Alliance of Women Directors, SXSW, Women In Film (WIF) and The Black List.

	NYDF will host its next event, a fourth anniversary party, on Friday at the Aster in Hollywood. Six up-and-coming filmmakers will showcase their work to the crowd of industry insiders before participating in a Q&A.
	

	In addition to its events schedule, NYDF has expanded its reach beyond L.A. through “Daddy Dailies,” a podcast spotlighting women and nonbinary creatives. Guests have included Patty Jenkins, Diablo Cody, Meaghan Oppenheimer, Mary Bronstein, Ashley Nicole Black, Lena Khan, Hannah McMechan and Danya Jimenez. NYDF also publishes its annual Daddy’s List, which highlights emerging filmmakers to watch. Notable alumni include Haley Z. Boston (showrunner of “Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen”), director Giselle Bonilla (the 2026 Sundance standout “The Musical”) and director Gia-Rayne B. Harris (“Bridgerton”).

	The organization plans to use the increased funding via Film Independent to expand its screenings and educational programming, develop more workshops and resources for emerging filmmakers, build out its advisory leadership and organizational infrastructure, grow the “Daddy Dailies” podcast, strengthen its presence at major film festivals and create more direct pathways connecting filmmakers with professional opportunities.

title: Tatiana Huezo, Elisa Miller Bring New Films to the Morelia Film Festival’s 12th Impulso Morelia
description: A mix of established and first-time Mexican filmmakers are presenting their upcoming projects at the Morelia Film Festival’s 12th Impulso Morelia, w
body:
A mix of established and first-time Mexican filmmakers are presenting their upcoming projects at the Morelia Film Festival’s 12th Impulso Morelia, which features works-in-progress in varied stages of post-production.

	Out of the six entries, selected from around 90 submissions, three are women, led by Tatiana Huezo (“Tempestad,” “Prayers for the Stolen”) and Eliza Miller (“Hurricane Season”), both acclaimed for their award-winning pics and backed by leading producer Pimienta Films (“Roma”).  
	

	“I think there’s a really interesting variety this year and a sensibility that runs throughout the entire selection. The characters aren’t simply vulnerable—they’re contradictory and fragile. But across all the films, there’s a desire to approach these characters with great empathy. They speak, in different ways, to the vulnerability of being human,” said Impulso head, Andrea Stavenhagen.


	“Impulso is more than just a space for exhibition; it’s a space for dialogue, for listening and exchange—not simply for showcasing films. What matters most to us is that the discussion and feedback we receive can help enrich and refine the films before they reach the public,” she told Variety.

	“It’s a work-in-progress forum in the fullest sense: an opportunity to receive guidance on the editing, discuss the current cut and engage in dialogue with fellow filmmakers and industry professionals. It’s about opening things up and allowing other filmmakers and professionals to contribute to the process of finding the film’s final form.”

	Unspooling over Oct. 18-20, these selected pics-in-post will be assessed by a panel of industry experts led by Ted Hope, co-founder of The Good Machine, which worked with major talent including Ang Lee; notable Mexican producer-writer Julio Chavezmontes of Piano (“The Meltdown”); Tribeca director Cara Cusumano; French multi-hyphenate Sandrine Dumas and Carlos R. Rios, director of D’A – Festival de Cinema de Barcelona.
	

	Various awards in cash and kind are at stake, led by the José María Riba Impulso Morelia 12 Award, presented by Cinépolis Distribution and Profest 2026, which comprises a cash prize of $14,740. (250,000 pesos) to cover post-production and/or promotional processes and services. The award will be granted by the international panel.

	Estudios Churubusco Azteca will award image and sound post-production services valued at $41,280 (700,000 pesos) which may be allocated entirely to a single project or divided between two projects.

	Estudios Splendor Omnia and Caffeine will also award post production services in kind, valid for two years.

	The winner of the José María Riba Award LatAm also wins a promotional campaign valued at $1,500 from the digital media platform LatAm Cinema.

	Impulso Morelia 12 Projects:

	“Galerna,” Tatiana Huezo

	Prod. Nicolás Celis, Tatiana Huezo, María Zamora/ Production companies: Pimienta Films, Elastica Films

	Huezo’s second fiction film, it follows Lúa and Noé whose mission is to cast first-time actors for a sci-fi pic.  It’s their first time to work together and Noé has some doubts about Lúa’s qualifications. Traveling through remote regions, they discover a Mexico that both welcomes and unsettles them, forcing them to confront their fears and prejudices while testing their resilience, tolerance and vulnerability.

	“Homeboys,” Alonso Garibay, Alejandro Bernal

	Prod. Camila Aguirre Beltrán / Production companies: Norteña del Sur, Documotora

	This debut feature documentary centers on Roberto Hernández, “Mr. Lucky,” who was deported to a country he barely knew. After surviving prison, addiction and displacement, he founded La Casa de Vida, a shelter that for 15 years sought to help deported gang members and ex-convicts. When a grave crisis threatens his life’s work, Roberto must face his past and ponder whether it makes sense to keep going.



	

					‘Homeboys’
	



	“Katechon,” Javier Toscano

	Prod. Javier Toscano / Production company: Didascalia Films

	Documentary follows three human-rights activists from the Western Sahara, Kurdistan, and Palestine, weaving their struggles for freedom into a visual tapestry of memory, intimacy and desert landscapes, the film explores resilience and self-determination through a Global South lens.
	



	

					‘Katechon’
	



	“Legit” (“Legítima”), “Elisa Miller

	Prod. Nicolás Celis/ Production company: Pimienta Films

	Based on actual events, it follows the case of Yakiri Rubio who is kidnapped and raped by two brothers. Instead of backing her, the courts convict her for killing her attacker in self-defense. With the help of her charismatic lawyer, Ana Katiria Suárez, she fights the misogynistic and patriarchal system to secure her release.



	

					‘Legit’
	



	“Raká,” Teresa Camou

	Prod. Yuli Margarita Rodríguez, Teresa Camou Guerrero/ Production companies: EFICINE, Teresa Camou Guerrero, La Furia Cine, Avalancha Studio

	Documentary. The tree serves as the story’s central metaphor: like the pines of the Sierra Tarahumara, Miguel (81) and Rosa (79), a Rarámuri couple, are deeply rooted in a land marked by violence and deforestation. Their story follows their enduring commitment to restoring the rivers and forests, sustaining the cycle of rain and life.



	

					‘Raka’
									RAUL_FERNANDO_PEREZ_LIRA
	



	“Springtime” (“Primavera”), Alfredo Mendoza Aguilar

	Prod. Sally Donette Talavera Sores/ Production companies: Fontana Films, Oriente Cine

	A debut fiction feature, it centers on Maria Carmela who contemplates suicide as a way to escape from her all-consuming depression and debilitating illness but cannot bring herself to do it.

	When she meets Fito, a troubled, drug-addicted teen estranged from his family and community, she offers him a life-changing pact: help her die, and she’ll give him a reason to change his own life.



	

					‘Springtime’

title: HBO Max Banks on Upcoming Genre Thriller ‘Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: HBO Max is firing up its Latin American slate with psychological thriller “Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer,” currently shooting in Mexico City. The
body:
HBO Max is firing up its Latin American slate with psychological thriller “Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer,” currently shooting in Mexico City. The new HBO original series is produced by Exile Content and has Mexico’s Humberto Hinojosa (“The Head of Joaquín Murrieta,” “Luis Miguel: The Series”) serving as the showrunner as well as co-directing alongside J.M. Cravioto (“El Chapo”).

	Based on one of Mexico’s most infamous criminal cases, “Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer,” burrows into the investigation that riveted the country as the hunt for a killer who targeted elderly women intensified. 
	

	The series “combines the suspense and tension of a compelling crime thriller with a distinctly Mexican perspective that is woven throughout the story,” said Mariano César, head of general entertainment content, Warner Bros. Discovery Latin America & U.S. Hispanic. 


	According to Hinojosa, from the moment he read the material handed to him by Exile Content’s Arturo Sampson, he felt they could create a series with strong thriller elements – police, investigation, a serial killer, all wrapped in an intriguing, entertaining plot.

	“It’s uncommon in Spanish-language storytelling, particularly in Mexico, to see popular, culturally significant cases wrapped in a genre-driven story where suspense and thriller elements take center stage,” Hinojosa told Variety, adding: “I found the series’ willingness to explore darker corners particularly compelling, while always showing that, no matter how dark things become, there is still a glimmer of light.”
	

	“Mexico is such a surreal country where practically anything can happen. The truth can’t always surpass fiction, and in this case, that’s exactly what happens. The story surrounding our characters is fascinating, but there’s also a strong thriller and suspense element that carries through all six episodes. For me, it was a fantastic opportunity to develop the tone, build the characters and shape how we wanted the series to look and feel, as well as the experience we wanted the audience to have.”

	Said Cravioto: “It’s a premium thriller that can resonate not only in Mexico, but anywhere in the world. It draws from Mexico’s unique cultural imagination while embracing sophisticated genre conventions and a powerful cinematic approach.”



	

					Behind the Scenes: ‘Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer’  Courtesy of HBO Max/ HBO
									ALDO AYLLON
	



	“Being part of building that atmosphere has been incredibly rewarding – and challenging. The visual world Beto created with the cinematography and production design teams demands a sharp eye and constant exploration. Getting the shots, the sets and the rhythm of the series has been the greatest challenge—the day-to-day struggle to achieve that level of quality and such a high standard. We want the series to stand out and break away from the conventions of national productions and I’m very proud to be part of it.”

	“We believe the strength of the story and the caliber of the talent behind it will resonate with audiences both in Latin America and around the world,” said César.

	To be launched worldwide, “Mataviejitas: The Serial Killer” is among the upcoming HBO Originals from Latin America alone. Under the baton of Sarah Aubrey, head of original programming for HBO Max, critically acclaimed shows such as “The Pitt” and “Hacks” have garnered 75 Emmy nominations and 17 wins alone. In December, the much-anticipated Harry Potter series based on the books is set to launch.

	Like its closest rivals Netflix, Disney+ and Prime Video, which recently announced a $2 billion-plus investment in the region, HBO Max continues to invest in local programming in a bid to boost viewership and audience engagement.

	Upcoming Latin American Shows:

	“The Flores Massacre” (“La Masacre de Flores”) (Argentina)
	

	Docuseries – Revisits one of Argentina’s most infamous criminal cases. 

	“Carnival Poet” (“Poeta Canival”) (Mexico)

	Docuseries – Follows José Luis Calva Zepeda, known as the Cannibal Poet, whose arrest followed the discovery of a shocking crime, revealing how a charismatic and unsettling man became a monster.

	 “Carlota” (Mexico) 

	New drama series produced by Sony Pictures Television and inspired by the life of Carlota of Hapsburg, the last Empress of Mexico. Stars Belinda, the Spanish-born Mexican Latin pop star as the titular Carlota.

	“Collision” (“Colission”) (Mexico)

	After years abroad, Zoé returns to Mexico following her father’s death, determined to inherit his legacy and family business. But her mother, Belén, has already taken control and refuses to step aside. As their rivalry intensifies, old wounds resurface, secrets emerge and an investigation raises one question: Was his death really an accident?

	“Don Ramon” (Mexico)

	A spin-off from the wildly popular 1970s Televisa sitcom “El Chavo del Ocho”

	“Tragedy in the Corregidora” (“Tragedia en la Corregidora) (Mexico)

	Docuseries – Revisits the events of 2022, when the historic rivalry between Querétaro and Atlas soccer clubs triggered a battle that forever changed Mexican soccer (futbol) history.

	“City of God: The Fight Rages On” Season 2 (Brazil)

	Produced by O2 Filmes, Season 2 continues Paulo Lins’ literary work through photographer Buscapé’s perspective. Set in the early 2000s, the series follows the characters’ lives while using flashbacks from the film to revisit their memories.

title: Larenz Tate Boards Vault, New Streaming and Distribution Platform for Indie Filmmakers (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Michael” star Larenz Tate is expanding his influence behind the camera by joining the team behind Vault, a new streaming and distribution platform
body:
“Michael” star Larenz Tate is expanding his influence behind the camera by joining the team behind Vault, a new streaming and distribution platform focused on empowering indie filmmakers. 

	Tate has teamed up with Kenneth Gifford, founder of the Newark International Film Festival, for the project, along with his brothers and business partners Larron and Lahmard Tate. Collectively, their mission, as described in a press release announcing Vault’s launch, is to “connect creators with global audiences,” with the platform designed to “give independent filmmakers greater access, control and ownership in an evolving entertainment landscape.” 
	

	Vault, which is already live, serves as a hub for independent film, television, documentaries, short-form content and music. The platform offers free access to viewers, as well as a subscription model that provides a more curated viewing experience. (More than 50,000 subscribers have signed up to date, according to the release.) Filmmakers can host content on the platform at no cost and determine which films, programs or episodes are available for free or placed behind a paywall, while maintaining control over pricing, monetization and revenue. Vault also offers filmmakers tools to market their projects: creators can assign their own genres and generate shareable, interactive branded landing pages for individual titles, intended to create opportunities for discovery, promotion and audience engagement.


	“The entertainment industry continues to evolve, but too often filmmakers and creatives are left with limited control over how their work is distributed, monetized and ultimately seen,” Larenz Tate said in a statement. “With VAULT, we have an opportunity to shift that dynamic — putting more power back into the hands of creators while giving their stories the ability to reach audiences around the world. It’s about ownership, access and creating a platform where great work can find its audience.”
	

	Tate embarks on this endeavor after more than four decades in the entertainment business, starring in classic films like “Love Jones,” “Dead Presidents,” “Ray” and “Girls Trip,” as well as in the massively successful “Power” franchise on Starz. He most recently starred in “Michael,” portraying Motown Records founder Berry Gordy. 

	Vault marks the latest expansion of Tate’s work alongside Larron and Lahmard Tate through their TateMen Entertainment. The company previously partnered with AMC Global Networks, ALLBLK and Starz on emerging filmmaker programs, and launched film, television and creative industry initiatives in their hometown of Chicago.

title: Edinburgh TV Festival Takeaways: YouTube’s Rise, Commissioning Landscape and Move to Manchester
description: This year’s Edinburgh TV Festival was one of the buzziest, a somewhat ironic fact given it’s also the last. From next year the TV festival, which fi
body:
This year’s Edinburgh TV Festival was one of the buzziest, a somewhat ironic fact given it’s also the last. From next year the TV festival, which first originated in the Scottish city fifty years ago, is moving to Manchester.

	The move was inevitably the talk of this year’s edition, with many genuinely emotional at the close of such a significant chapter. But with the TV business under more pressure than ever, it wasn’t the main topic of conversation. Read on for Variety’s top takeaways from this year’s fest.
	
	
		The Rise of YouTube	

	There was no getting away from YouTube this year, not least because its EMEA boss Pedro Pina delivered this year’s keynote McTaggart lecture, in which he tried to persuade a suspicious if not outwardly hostile audience that the Silicon Valley platform is “not the villain.”


	But the video sharing giant came up in nearly every other panel, particularly those spotlighting the U.K.’s traditional public service broadcasters, who weren’t afraid to make their views known. ITV entertainment boss Kevin Lygo scoffed at Pina’s £3 million pledge for U.K. content (“I did have a little chortle,” Lygo said. “You think, well, we [spend] £1.2 billion every year.”) Meanwhile Channel 5 boss Ben Frow claimed PSBs still offer a bigger platform than YouTube while the network itself doesn’t “make nearly as much money on YouTube” compared to traditional avenues.

	Unsurprisingly, the BBC’s new director-general Matt Brittin – Pina’s former boss at Google – was not as dismissive about his former employer, even suggesting the BBC could come up with its own local-news version to stay relevant.
	

	Love it or hate it, with its viewing figures fast overtaking traditional broadcasters’, YouTube is now undeniably a part of the U.K.’s broadcasting ecosystem.
	
		Duty of Care	

	With yet another contributor welfare scandal having hit British broadcasting this year in the form of Channel 4’s “Married at First Sight” U.K., duty of care continues to be front of mind. On the Channel 4 panel, director of content strategy Kiran Nataraja sidestepped questions about the scandal, citing two ongoing investigations, but her colleague Shaminder Nahal, head of specialist factual, was quizzed over another show, “Virgin Island.” “We review everything all the time,” Nahal said. “We’ve got a whole team of experts there.”

	On the Netflix panel, director of unscripted Syeda Irtizaali was also questioned about duty of care on upcoming show “Netflix, Will You Marry Me?” in which viewers dictate the participant’s decisions. “We really thought hard about the duty of care,” Irtizaali claimed. “It’s at the center of our editorial.” Elsewhere, the festival hosted a panel titled “Too Big to Fail: Reality TV’s Duty of Care Reckoning” featuring former “Geordie Shore” cast member Vicky Pattison.

	The question, of course, is all the awareness around the topic enough to prevent another scandal in the future? Only time will tell.
	
		Who’s Still Commissioning?	

	For the independent producers in the audience, many of whom had paid large sums to attend the festival, one of the key questions was who is still commissioning, particularly in this era of aggressive consolidation.

	The answers were an indictment of the state of the industry. The U.K.’s public service broadcasters are, by and large, in a sorry state. Channel 4’s Kiran Nataraja, director of content strategy, said the network is “still open for business” but admitted that commissioning was “slower” at the moment as they wait to find a new director of programs, after incumbent Ian Katz leaves in October. At Paramount-owned Channel 5, Ben Frow said he was still commissioning but there were fewer opportunities for higher-end budgets. “I can only do very, very few [shows at] £400,000 pounds an hour, but I can do a lot with £35,000 pounds an hour,” he explained. 
	

	With its acquisition by Sky looming (the deal is currently going through the regulatory process), ITV entertainment boss Kevin Lygo was keen to reassure producers the network is continuing to function as normal, although with its £2.1 billion ITV Studios output deal, it’s questionable how much space there remains for indies.

	Over at the streamers, however, there is no sense of a slowdown. In advance of its Edinburgh panel Netflix compiled a list at all of its upcoming re-commissions – which included “Black Mirror” Season 8, “The Gentlemen” Season 3 and “Legends” Season 2 among others – before announcing a further nine new shows during the panel itself, including two “Top Boy” spin-offs, a Roald Dahl series and a new vengeance drama starring Kate Winslet. When, during the panel, U.K. content chief Anne Mensah was asked whether Netflix was still commissioning, she replied “Oh my god!” and added “Completely.” Over at Prime Video, head of international originals Nicole Clemens was equally clear the streamer is looking for new content, while at Disney+ head of content Angela Jain cited a target set by Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro to triple the number of local originals globally.
	
		The Move to Manchester	

	The TV Festival’s impending move to Manchester was one of the foremost topics of conversation at this year’s edition. The festival has been in Edinburgh since its inception in the Scottish capital 50 years ago and almost everyone Variety spoke to about the move expressed some disappointment. While there was some sympathy for the reasons behind the move – a week in Edinburgh is inevitably expensive, particularly since it takes place during the renowned Edinburgh Fringe, putting travel and accommodation at a premium – numerous questions remain regarding the move. Foremost is when will the Manchester version take place, given dates are still to be confirmed?

	In Edinburgh it has always occupied the last week of August, timed between the traditional summer holiday lull and the busy fall/winter season, which encompasses the Royal Television Society conference in September, followed by Mipcom in Cannes in October and Content London in the first week of December. “Where will a Manchester-based TV Festival fit into that?” was the question many were asking.
	

	Adding to the squeeze, the Edinburgh Fringe has become an increasingly important part of the TV ecosystem, with hits ranging from “Fleabag” to “Baby Reindeer” originating at the Fringe. Last year it was also a key pipeline for the producers of “Saturday Night Live” U.K., who scoured the festival looking for new comedy talent for the series. Despite the cost, part of Edinburgh TV Festival’s pull has always been its overlap with the fringe, enabling commissioners and producers to check out what’s going on on the ground as well as taking meetings.

	But as well as practical reasons, there are emotional ones, with Edinburgh offering a history and charm that sparks creativity. As one publicist lamented of Manchester, “No cobbles!” Sky’s head of entertainment Philip Edgar-Jones (who happens to be a Scot) was so overcome by the prospect, at the end of Sky’s panel he asked for the lights to come up so he could take a commemorative selfie with his fellow panellists and the audience in the Pentland theater.

	Scotland’s creative bodies, meanwhile, aren’t taking the loss lying down, with plans already afoot to fill the gap with their own media conference. Watch this space.

title: Kirill Sokolov to Direct Animated Feature ‘Alone in the Ocean,’ About Freediver Slava Kurilov’s Famed Escape From Soviet Union (EXCLUSIVE)

body:
Kirill Sokolov, the Russian filmmaker known for violent dark comedies such as “Why Don’t You Just Die!” and his recent Hollywood debut “They Will Kill You,” is set to direct his first animated feature. 

	Backed by Lazy Sunday and The Media Company, “Alone in the Ocean” will be based on the “extraordinary life and legendary escape story” of Slava Kurilov, who fled from the U.S.S.R. in 1974. 


	An oceanographer and experienced diver, Kurilov dreamed of joining international expeditions and exploring the world’s oceans, but opportunities to work abroad remained out of reach. Over time, his desire to pursue his life’s work became inseparable from a larger longing for personal freedom.
	

	However, in December 1974, Kurilov found a way out. He bought a ticket for a 20-day Soviet cruise from Vladivostok toward the equator and back. Because the ship was not scheduled to call at any foreign ports, passengers did not require exit visas. Kurilov studied the route and planned to jump overboard as the ship passed near the Philippines.


	But the escape did not go according to plan. Kurilov jumped from the cruise ship into the Pacific farther from the Philippine islands than he had intended and spent nearly three days swimming alone before reaching Siargao.

	Kurilov would later describe those days at sea as among the happiest of his life. His experience became the basis of his autobiographical book “Alone in the Ocean,” first published in full in 2004, after his death following a diving accident in 1998.

	The film adaptation of “Alone in the Ocean” was original developed as a live-action feature. But over several years of development the filmmakers and producers came to see contemporary animation techniques as a way of going beyond a literal reconstruction of Kurilov’s journey‚ allowing the film to move between physical reality, memory and inner experience, and to capture both the scale of the ocean and the intensely personal nature of his pursuit of freedom.
	

	The feature will combine a range of contemporary filmmaking and animation techniques, including live-action footage, motion capture, rotoscoping, 2D and 3D animation and water simulation. Rather than committing to a single visual technique, the filmmakers plan to use different forms to move between the physical reality of Kurilov’s journey and his memories, perceptions and inner states.

	“I’ve lived with this story for a long time,” said Sokolov, who was recently tapped to direct Netflix’s upcoming sci-fi action feature “Blur.” “When we started discussing the possibility of animation, I realized that it could open the story up in a completely different way. It gives us the freedom to make Kurilov’s physical journey and his inner experience part of the same cinematic language, to make it vivid and emotional.”

	Roman Sokolov will serve as art director on  “Alone in the Ocean,” shaping the film’s visual language alongside Kirill Sokolov and the animation team. His work includes collaborations with acclaimed animator Konstantin Bronzit on Academy Award-nominated animated shorts.

	“Alone in the Ocean” is being produced by Artem Vasilyev (Lazy Sunday), Roman Borisevich, Didier Lupfer (The Media Company), with Alan Keane (Lazy Sunday) serving as creative producer. The producers are currently in discussions with a number of potential partners across Europe as the project moves forward.

	“We acquired the rights to Slava Kurilov’s book quite a long time ago, and we have spent years looking for the right way to bring this story to the screen,” said Vasilyev. “We’re also very happy to continue working with Kirill after our film together ‘No Looking Back.’ We explored several different approaches to ‘Alone in the Ocean,’ and animation finally gave us a new and incredibly exciting way into the material. Kurilov’s story is very specific, but the desire at its center, to be free to pursue the life and work you believe in, is universal. We believe this can be a film that speaks to audiences in many different countries.”

	Added Lupfer: “Slava Kurilov’s incredible adventure is a subject that has always fascinated me ever since I read his book. ‘Alone in the Ocean’ is not only a story with tremendous cinematic potential, but also an adaptation that perfectly aligns with The Media Company’s ambitions to reach an audience that is increasingly eager for exciting and original stories.”
	

	Borisevich said: “To me, Kurilov was a man who refused to live by someone else’s script or accept the limits imposed by his time and circumstances. His leap into the ocean was a step into the unknown, taken to claim the right to choose his own course. Alone with the open sea, he seems to have found what he had sought all his life: a sense of true freedom. In that solitude, there is something that goes beyond a struggle for survival — a rare moment when freedom ceases to be a dream and becomes a lived reality.”

	Lazy Sunday recently wrapped principal photography on horror-thriller “A Most Delightful Game” by Boman Modine and assumed management of the non-dialogue animated series “Beep Boop’s” IP, alongside its continuing work across animation and live-action production.

	Further production details will be announced in the coming months.

Andrew Tate's Sex Trafficking Case
                          Girlfriend Was Not Pregnant In Court
                          ... Suffered Miscarriages
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 28, 2026
                            6:41 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Andrew Tate's girlfriend testified Thursday in his federal sex trafficking case in Miami, but she was not pregnant with his child, contrary to reports -- and she has suffered past miscarriages as the couple tries to expand their family, according to his lawyer.
      
    
            Tate's attorney, Joseph McBride, tells TMZ ... the media got it all wrong when they reported that Tate's girlfriend of 6 years, Natasha Sesay, was pregnant with their second child while testifying Thursday at Andrew's federal bail hearing in an effort to get him released on bond.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            McBride says the two are expecting their second child via surrogacy because they've been trying to have kids together for some time ... going with a surrogate after Natasha suffered "brutal miscarriages."
      

            Still, McBride says, the pair are committed to having a loving family. They have a child who is 8 1/2 months old and the baby was born through IVF.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            McBride also said Natasha loves Andrew despite his misogynistic online persona because she understands the nuances of his statements -- and disagrees with him at times.
      
    
            The lawyer also pointed out that "she's no pushover" and her testimony yesterday was both "captivating" and meant a lot to Andrew.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            McBride said Natasha is so deeply in love with Andrew that she flew all the way from Dubai to try to get him released from jail. So far, that hasn't happened.
      
    
            As you know, Andrew and his brother, Tristan, were arrested by the feds in July and tossed in a Miami federal jail. They have been fighting extradition to the UK, where they were hit with a smorgasbord of 59 charges involving rape and sex trafficking.

                          Serious Brain Injuries Lead To Shutdown
body:
Six Flags Roller Coaster
                          Serious Brain Injuries Lead To Shutdown
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 28, 2026
                            8:36 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A popular Six Flags roller coaster linked to two deaths and recent traumatic brain injuries in California is being grounded.
      
    
            A new CNN investigation reviewed records tied to the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia and found more than a dozen riders suffered serious injuries or hospitalizations over the years ... including multiple brain injuries.
      
    
            Two women were hospitalized just six days apart in July after riding X2 -- and both needed emergency brain surgery.
      

            One collapsed after getting off the coaster ... while the other is still dealing with headaches, fatigue and other effects from brain damage.
      
    
            CNN also found a 22-year-old man died after riding X2 ... with his family saying he had been healthy beforehand.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags has maintained the 24-year-old coaster undergoes daily inspections and a normal rider using it properly would not suffer a traumatic brain injury. The coaster is currently closed.
      
    
            Another death was linked to the coaster in 2010 ... when Hilda Farias died after riding X2 ... though medical experts said multiple factors were at play, including an existing brain abnormality.
      
    
            Suddenly, keeping your hands and feet inside the ride at all times doesn't sound like the only thing to worry about. Thrill ride, indeed.
